title: Stack and heap
objectives: Explain object lifetimes on the stack and the heap.
Pair every `new` with the right `delete`, and spot a leak.

screens.title: Two million prices

state.caption: Locals get 8 MB in total, here and on a typical Linux desk

screens.question: Which program crashes?

options.text: A only
Both: 16 MB does not fit in 8 MB
options.why: B's vector keeps its two million `double`s somewhere else; only the small vector object is a local.

options.text: B only
options.why: A's array is a local, all 16 MB of it, so A is the one that does not fit.

options.text: Neither
options.why: A asks for 16 MB of locals in an 8 MB region, so it runs off the end.

hints.text: Where does each program put the two million `double`s?
A's array is itself a local. B's local is a `std::vector`, which holds a pointer to its elements.
A needs 16 MB of locals and has 8 MB: it crashes. B's elements live elsewhere, so B runs.

feedback.correct: Only the array is a 16 MB local.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which program makes the 16 MB a local variable.

byKey.both: B's elements are not locals. The vector object is small; it points at its elements elsewhere.

explain.text: A's array is a local, so all 16 MB must fit in the 8 MB for locals. It overflows: this browser reports "memory access out of bounds", and g++ on Linux says `Segmentation fault`. B's vector object is 12 bytes here; its elements live elsewhere, so B runs.

screens.title: Frames come and go
screens.question: Step through the program until no frames are left.

ops.label: `main` prints `v`
ops.why: `v` comes from `value`, so `main` must call `value` first.

ops.label: `value` returns
ops.why: `value` needs `m`, so it must call `mid` first.

ops.label: `value` returns
ops.why: Only the frame on top can finish, and `mid` is on top.

ops.label: `mid` returns again
ops.why: `mid`'s frame, with its `bid` and `ask`, was removed when it returned.

ops.label: `value` returns again
ops.why: `value` has finished; its frame and its `m` are gone.

hints.text: A call adds a frame on top; a return removes the top frame.
Only the frame on top can finish.
`main` calls `value`, `value` calls `mid`. Then `mid` returns, `value` returns, and `main` prints and ends.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only the frame on top can return.

explain.text: Frames pile up as calls start and come off the top as they return. When `mid` returned, its `bid` and `ask` were gone. This pile is the **stack**: every local lives in a frame and dies at its function's `}`.

screens.title: Memory that outlives a call

state.caption: `p` in `make_price`'s frame, `q` in `main`'s; the `double` on the heap

screens.question: Is reading `*q` in `main` safe?

options.text: Yes: the `double` is on the heap and lives until `delete q`
No: it died when `make_price` returned
options.why: That is true of locals. Only `p` was a local; the `double` that `new` made is on the heap.

options.text: No: `q` is a copy of `p`, so it points somewhere else
options.why: Copying a pointer copies the address. `q` holds the same address `p` held.

hints.text: Which objects live in `make_price`'s frame, and which does `new` create?
`p` is in the frame; the `double` is on the heap.
When `make_price` returns, `p` dies. The heap `double` stays, and `q` holds its address until `delete q`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the pointer `p` from the `double` it points at.

byKey.dies: Only `p` lived in the frame. The `double` came from `new`, so it is on the heap.

explain.text: `p` lived in `make_price`'s frame and died at its `}`, but it had already handed its address to `q`. The `double` from `new` is on the heap, so `*q` reads 101.5. `delete q` ends it; a heap object's lifetime is yours to manage.

canvas.caption: After the call: `p` is gone, the heap `double` is not

screens.title: Stack or heap
screens.prose: A local lives on the stack, even when it is a pointer or a vector. What `new` makes, and what a vector holds, lives on the heap.
screens.question: Fill in where each lives while `main` runs: stack or heap.

hints.text: Every variable declared inside `main` is a local. What do the pointer and the vector point at?
`buf` holds an address; `new double[n]` made what it points at.
`n`, `buf` and `prices` are locals: stack. `buf[0]` came from `new[]`, and `prices[0]` is inside the vector's buffer: heap.

feedback.correct: The handles are on the stack; the data is on the heap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate each local from what it points at.

explain.text: `n`, the pointer `buf` and the vector object `prices` are locals in `main`'s frame. The 1,000 `double`s from `new double[n]` and the vector's 1,000 elements are on the heap. A vector object is 12 bytes in this browser and 24 on a 64-bit desk, whatever its size.

screens.title: A leak

lines: Direct leak of 8000 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 8000 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s).
params.title: Terminal: one call to sum_prices(1000)

screens.question: A backtest calls `sum_prices(1000)` once a day for 2,500 trading days. How many MB leak? Take 1 MB as 1,000,000 bytes.

hints.text: How many bytes does one call leak?
Line 3 of the report gives one call's leak.
Each call leaks 1,000 × 8 = 8,000 bytes. Times 2,500 calls is 20,000,000 bytes, or 20 MB.

feedback.correct: 8,000 bytes a day, 20 MB in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply one call's leak by the number of calls.

byKey.one: That is one call. The backtest calls it 2,500 times.
byKey.bytes: That is the count in bytes. Divide by 1,000,000.
byKey.noeight: You counted one byte per price. Each `double` is 8 bytes.

explain.text: Each call leaks one `new double[1000]`, 8,000 bytes, and line 5 of the report names `sum_prices` at `leak.cpp:2`. Over 2,500 days that is 20 MB that is never given back. In a server that runs for weeks, leaks like this end in an out-of-memory crash.

screens.title: Which delete
screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: `new[]` must be paired with `delete[]`; plain `delete` is undefined behaviour
Nothing: the program ran and exited with 0
options.why: This browser build is forgiving. Pairing `new[]` with plain `delete` is undefined, and a desk build with checks stops on it.

options.text: It frees only the first 8 bytes and leaks the rest
options.why: It is not a tidy partial free. It is undefined behaviour: the allocator may corrupt itself or crash.

options.text: It should be `free(px)`
options.why: `free` pairs with `malloc`, not with `new[]`. Mixing them is undefined too.

hints.text: How was `px` allocated?
`new double[1000]` has brackets.
Every `new` pairs with `delete`, and every `new[]` with `delete[]`. Mixing them is undefined.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the form of `delete` to the form of `new`.

byKey.nothing: This browser build is forgiving. A desk build with `-fsanitize=address` reports "alloc-dealloc-mismatch" here.

explain.text: `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`. clang warns at compile time, and a desk build with AddressSanitizer stops with "alloc-dealloc-mismatch". The browser build ran it silently: that is luck, not correctness.

screens.title: A heap buffer from input
screens.prose: Finish the program. It reads `n`, then `n` prices into a heap buffer, prints their sum to 2 decimals, and frees the buffer. `new double[0]` is allowed: it returns a pointer you must not read through, but must still free.
screens.question: Complete the program.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs your program 5 times with different input. A hidden leak checker counts every `new[]`: if a block never reaches `delete[]`, the program ends with status 1 and the test fails.

hints.text: Two loops, or one: read each `px[i]`, then add them up.
`std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2)` prints two decimals.
Read with `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) std::cin >> px[i];`, sum into `total`, print it, and finish with `delete[] px;`.

feedback.generic: Not yet. The results under the editor say which test failed.

byKey.test-1: If the output is right but the test failed with status 1, the leak checker fired: `new[]` needs `delete[]`, not `delete`.

explain.text: The buffer from `new double[n]` lives on the heap until `delete[] px`. With `n` = 0 the loops never run and the program prints 0.00, but the zero-length block must still be freed. Plain `delete px` is what the leak checker caught.

screens.title: From a C buffer to a vector
screens.prose: Exchange feeds often have a C interface: you hand over a buffer and the feed fills it. `fill_ticks(double* out, int n)` is hidden above your code. `std::vector<double> out(buf, buf + n)` copies a pointer range into a vector.
screens.question: Write `read_ticks(n)`: fill a `new[]` buffer, return its prices as a vector, and leave no leak.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests. The hidden leak checker fails a test whose program ends with a `new[]` block that never reached `delete[]`.

hints.text: Allocate, fill, copy, free, return: in that order.
Free the buffer after copying it into the vector, never before.
`double* buf = new double[n]; fill_ticks(buf, n); std::vector<double> out(buf, buf + n); delete[] buf; return out;`

feedback.correct: The vector owns a copy; the buffer is freed.
feedback.generic: Not yet. The results under the editor say which test failed.

explain.text: The vector copies the `n` prices into its own heap buffer, so the `new[]` buffer can be freed before returning. `fill_ticks(out.data(), n)` on a vector of size `n` would skip the manual buffer entirely: the vector frees its own memory, which is the next lesson.

screens.title: Where things live
screens.question: A recursion 10,000,000 calls deep stops with "call stack exhausted". What ran out?

options.text: The stack: every call still waiting holds a frame
The heap
options.why: Frames are not on the heap. The heap is for `new` and for containers' elements.

options.text: Time: it ran too long
options.why: Each frame takes stack space, and 10 million waiting frames do not fit, whatever the time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does each waiting call keep its frame?

explain.text: Each call that has not returned keeps a frame on the stack. Ten million of them need far more than a few MB, so the stack overflows. A loop, or a vector used as your own stack, keeps depth off the call stack.

screens.title: The life of a heap double
screens.prose: Back to `make_price` and `main`, where `main` does `double* q = make_price();`, reads `*q`, then calls `delete q;`.
screens.question: Put the events in the order they happen.

lines.text: `main`'s frame is pushed: the program starts
`make_price`'s frame is pushed on top: `main` called it
`new` puts 101.5 on the heap; `p` in the top frame holds its address
`make_price`'s frame and `p` are popped; the heap `double` stays
`delete q` frees the heap `double`: `q` now dangles

hints.text: Frames come and go with calls; heap objects come and go with `new` and `delete`.
The heap object is created inside `make_price`, and outlives it.
Push `main`, push `make_price`, `new`, pop `make_price`, then `delete` in `main`.

feedback.correct: The heap object outlives the frame that made it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A frame must exist before code inside it runs `new`.

explain.text: The `double` is created while `make_price`'s frame is on top, survives that frame's pop, and ends only at `delete q`. After the `delete`, `q` still holds the old address: reading `*q` then would be undefined.

screens.title: A pricer's lattice
screens.prose: A binomial pricer needs `steps + 1` doubles of scratch space per price. A volatility calibration prices 50,000 options at 1,000 steps each, one after another.
screens.question: How should the pricer get its scratch space?

options.text: Hold a `std::vector<double>` member, sized once to `steps + 1` and reused for every price
`new double[steps + 1]` and `delete[]` inside every call
options.why: That works, but it pays for 50,000 trips to the allocator, and one missed `delete[]` leaks on every price.

options.text: A local array `double v[steps + 1]`
options.why: In standard C++ an array's size must be known at compile time, and a large local array can overflow the stack.

options.text: `new` once at start-up and never `delete`
options.why: It runs, but nothing owns the memory or frees it, and leak checkers flag it. The next lesson's tools give it an owner.

hints.text: The size is the same for every price. Why allocate it 50,000 times?
A member lives as long as the pricer object.
Size a vector once, then reuse its elements: one allocation, freed automatically when the pricer goes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the allocations each design makes, and ask who frees them.

explain.text: A vector member is allocated once and reused for all 50,000 prices, and it frees itself when the pricer is destroyed. Allocation in a hot loop costs time, and manual `new[]`/`delete[]` invites leaks. Desks preallocate lattices and buffers for exactly this reason.

ideas: Each call's locals live in its frame on the stack and die at its `}`. The stack is a few MB, so big arrays and very deep recursion overflow it.
`new` puts an object on the heap until you `delete` it: `new` with `delete`, `new[]` with `delete[]`, exactly once. A `new` with no `delete` leaks.
A vector object is a small local; its elements are on the heap. The browser build forgives mismatched or double deletes; a desk build with `-fsanitize=address` does not.

formula.name: Pairing allocations
formula.note: Never `delete` what `new` did not return, such as the address of a local.

summary.trap: Plain `delete` on memory from `new[]` is undefined behaviour, even when the program seems to run fine.

quiz.question: What is wrong here?

options.text: `price` is on the stack; `delete` is only for addresses `new` returned
Nothing: it frees `price` early
options.why: Stack objects are freed by their frame, at `}`. `delete` on one is undefined behaviour.

options.text: It leaks `price`
options.why: Nothing leaks: `price` goes with its frame. The bug is deleting memory that `new` never gave out.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Who created `price`, and who frees it?

explain.text: `price` lives in the frame and is freed at `}`. g++ warns "called on unallocated object 'price'", and the program aborts with `free(): invalid pointer`. This browser build ran it silently.

quiz.question: `int n = 0; double* p = new double[n];` What is true?

options.text: It is valid: `p` is not null, must not be read through, and still needs `delete[] p`
It returns `nullptr`
options.why: `new double[0]` returns a real, non-null pointer to zero elements.

options.text: It is undefined behaviour
options.why: Allocating zero elements is allowed. Reading `p[0]` would be undefined; freeing it is required.

feedback.correct: Zero elements, one block to free.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is a zero-length array allowed?

explain.text: A zero-length `new[]` is legal and returns a unique non-null pointer. There is nothing to read, but the block must still go to `delete[]`, or the leak checker counts it.

quiz.question: A strategy object is created at start-up and used until the program ends. Where can it live?

options.text: A local in `main`: `main`'s frame lasts the whole run
It must be on the heap, made with `new`
options.why: Nothing forces the heap. `main`'s frame exists from start to end, so a local there lives the whole session.

options.text: It cannot be a local: locals die too soon
options.why: Locals die at their function's `}`, and `main`'s `}` is the end of the program.

feedback.correct: `main`'s locals live as long as the program.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When does `main`'s frame end?

explain.text: A local in `main` lives until `main` returns, which is the end of the run. Other code can reach it through references you pass down. Heap allocation is for objects whose lifetime does not match a frame.

quiz.question: Inside a function, `std::vector<double> v(1000000);` Does it overflow the stack?

options.text: No: the elements are on the heap; only the small vector object is a local
Yes: 8 MB of locals is too much
options.why: The 8 MB of elements are on the heap. The local is the vector object, a few pointers.

feedback.correct: A vector's data is on the heap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which part of a vector is a local?

explain.text: `v` itself holds a few pointers (12 bytes here, 24 on a desk). Its million `double`s sit on the heap, so the stack is untouched. That is why large data goes in vectors, not local arrays.
